title: Sliding windows and warm episodes over freezer readings
objective_text: Count events in a sliding window that ends at each event, and group a run of matching events into one episode with gaps and islands.
scenario: Freezers send a temperature reading every few minutes. A reading above -15 °C is warm. Operations wants two things. The alarm fires when a freezer has 3 or more warm readings in the 10 minutes up to a warm reading, wherever those 10 minutes fall on the clock. The daily report lists each warm episode, which is a run of warm readings in a row that ends at the first reading that isn't warm.
verifies: Your SQL ran on this PC with DuckDB over a fixed set of readings and produced the expected sliding windows and warm episodes.
does_not_verify: Windowing in a running stream. This runs a batch query over stored readings, not an eventstream, KQL or Spark structured streaming.
Every output of a streaming sliding window. A streaming engine also emits a window when an event leaves it. Here a window is counted only when a warm reading arrives.
Which end of a sliding window an eventstream or Stream Analytics counts as inside. Here the exercise sets the rule itself.
Late readings and watermarks, which streaming engines add on top of these windows.

expected.result: The starter's final SELECT over freezer_windows, ordered by kind, device_id and window_start. Two sliding windows for F1 (3 and 4 readings) and four warm episodes.

validation.pass: The sliding windows and the warm episodes are right.
validation.fail: Check one kind at a time. For the sliding window, look at F2 at 11:10. For episodes, look at F1 at 10:08 and at F3 at 10:11.
A window appears twice or has no end.

hints: Warm means temp_c > -15. A reading of exactly -15.0 isn't warm.

For the sliding window, join the warm readings to themselves on device_id, keeping the other reading when it is after reading_ts - 10 minutes and not after reading_ts. Then group and keep count(*) >= 3.
RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '10 minutes' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW counts a reading exactly 10 minutes earlier too, which this exercise leaves out.
For episodes, number every reading of a device, and number it again within warm and not warm. Inside one run of warm readings the two numbers go up together, so their difference names the run.
A time gap between warm readings doesn't end an episode here. A reading that isn't warm does.
explanation: A sliding window has a fixed length but no fixed place on the clock. It is tied to the events, so it answers how many events happened in the last 10 minutes at any moment. A tumbling block from 10:00 to 10:10 can split a burst in two and miss the alarm, or join readings that are further apart than 10 minutes. Counting the last 3 rows instead of the last 10 minutes ignores time. Where the window starts matters too. Here a reading exactly 10 minutes earlier is outside. An episode isn't a time window at all. It's a run of rows that share a state, found with gaps and islands. Two row numbers, one over all of a device's readings and one within each state, rise together inside a run, so their difference is the same for every row of that run. A session window would cut on time gaps instead and treat a cold reading in between as if it weren't there. Eventstream's Group by covers tumbling, hopping and sliding windows, and its SQL operator uses the Stream Analytics query language.
troubleshooting: F2 shows a sliding window at 11:10. The window counts the reading at 11:00, which is exactly 10 minutes earlier. Keep only readings after reading_ts - 10 minutes.
F1 at 10:10 shows 3 readings, not 4. The window counts the last three rows, not the last 10 minutes.
F1 at 10:06 shows 4 readings. The window counts another device's readings, or readings that aren't warm.
F1 has one episode from 10:02 to 10:10. The 10:08 reading isn't warm, so it ends the first episode.
F3's episode runs to 10:11. -15.0 isn't above -15, so that reading isn't warm.
reset: Reset restores freezer_readings and drops freezer_windows.

Eventstream's Group by covers the tumbling, hopping and sliding patterns of Stream Analytics, and an eventstream supports the Stream Analytics query language (fabric/real-time-intelligence/event-streams/migrate-from-azure-event-hubs-stream-analytics).

Checked on Microsoft Learn 2026-11-23. A Stream Analytics sliding window outputs only when its content changes, when an event enters or exits, so every window has at least one event (azure/stream-analytics/stream-analytics-window-functions and stream-analytics-query/sliding-window-azure-stream-analytics). Neither page says which end of the window is inside, so the exercise states its own rule and doesn't claim it for Fabric.
The exercise counts a window only when a warm reading enters it, not when one leaves. That is stated in does_not_verify.
duckdb_lab has no hidden data, so an answer that types the expected rows as VALUES would pass. The data is small and each wrong answer moves at least one row.
